name: Welcome to Clinical Skills 1 course
text: Welcome to Clinical Skills 1 Course This course aims to introduce you to basic clinical and procedural skills such as hand hygiene, donning and doffing Personal Protective Equipment, principles of history taking and patient consultation, and finally, recording vital signs such as pulse and temperature. Dress and Behavior Expected in Clinical AreaIn order to gain and maintain the trust and confidence of patients, there are certain rules of behavior that a doctor or medical student must observe. If your standards of dress and behavior are professional and reasonably conservative you will be unlikely to cause offence or anxiety to your patients, and you will find that your relationships with them and with hospital staff will be easier. Students should be dressed in an appropriate and professional manner whilst on hospitals wards, at clinical skills sessions with patients or simulated patients and at OSCEs. • White coats are mandatory or surgical scrub• No low cut tops, no bare midriffs • No stilettos • No wrist watches, bracelets or wrist bands • No jewellery Except: o Rings – one single metal band, no stones o Earrings – small studs only o Necklaces – a simple chain if tucked inside clothing • No piercings (other than earrings) • Hair kept neat and tidy, long hair tied back, modest hair coloring/highlights only • Fingernails short and clean, no false nails • No food and drinks will be allowed in skills lab.• No Photos and videos will be allowed in skills lab.

name: Handout: Hand Hygiene
text: Review the session handout before clinical skills session on Hand Hygiene HAND HYGIENE Wash your hands with soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or visibly soiled with blood or other body fluids or after using the toilet . Preferred mean for routine hygienic hand antisepsis if hands are not visibly soiled . It is faster , more effective, and better tolerated by your hands than washing with soap and water. THANK YOU ILOs Understand the rational behind hand hygiene. State the indications for hand washing and antisepsis. Identify the WHO five moments for hand hygiene. Describe various hand hygiene techniques . Perform routine hand wash using the correct procedure. Perform alcohol hand rub using the correct procedure. Hand Hygiene Why? When? How? With what? WHY? WHEN? Before and after direct contact with patients. After removing gloves . Before manipulating an invasive device , with or without gloves. After coming into contact with liquids or bodily excretions , mucosa, non- intact skin or wound dressings. When caring for patients when moving from a contaminated area of the body to a clean one. After coming into contact with the inanimate objects (including medical equipment) in patient’s immediate area. WHO Five moments of HH WHEN & WHY? HOW? Techniques of Hand Hygiene PREPARATION (PRE-REQUISITE) Keep natural nails short (less than 0.5 cm long) Do not use artificial nails, or nail extensions when having direct contact with patients. Avoid excessive jewelry on fingers

name: Handout: PPE
text: PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT RESPIRATOR (N95) Indications of use Protect HCWs nose and mouth from large AND small droplets. RESPIRATOR (N95) How to don a respirator? Perform Hand hygiene Select a fit tested respirator RESPIRATOR (N95) How to doff a respirator? Perform Hand hygiene Lift the bottom elastic over your head first Then lift off the top elastic Discard in medical waste Perform Hand hygiene Indications of use Protection from contamination with blood, secretions, and excretions Anticipating contact with a patient’s mucous membranes (e.g., nasal, oral, genital area) Prevention of pathogen release from the hand into the work area during aseptic procedures. NON-STERILE GLOVES NON-STERILE GLOVES How to don gloves? Perform Hand hygiene Don gloves last Select correct type and size Insert hands into gloves Extend gloves over white coat/gown cuffs NON-STERILE GLOVES How to doff gloves? Grasp outside edge near wrist Peel away from hand, turning glove inside-out Hold in opposite gloved hand Slide ungloved finger under the wrist of the remaining glove Peel off from inside, creating a bag for both gloves Discard in medical waste Perform Hand hygiene REOMOVE GLOVES GLOVES DO DO NOT Change gloves if torn or heavily soiled Work from “clean to dirty” Change gloves after use on EACH patient Touch your face or adjust PPE with contaminated gloves Disard in appropriate receptacle Touch environmental surfaces except as necessary during patient care NEVER wash or reuse Indications of use help protect patients and healthcare providers from exposure of bodily fluids and infection. Isolation precautions Disposable Gown ILOs Provide information on the selection and use of PPE in healthcare settings Practice how to safely don and doff non-sterile gloves . Practice how to safely don and doff surgical masks . Practice how to safely don and doff N95 . Practice how to safely don and doff disposable gown . Disposable Gown How to don Gown? Fully cover torso from neck to knees, arms to end of wrists, and wrap around the back Fasten in back of neck and waist How to doff a gown? Gown front and sleeves are contaminated If your hands get contaminated during gown removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer Unfasten gown ties, taking care that sleeves don’t contact your body when reaching for ties Pull gown away from neck and shoulders, touching inside of gown only Turn gown inside out Fold or roll into a bundle and discard in a waste container Disposable Gown Removal of Gown Key points of PPE removal The key for PPE removal is to limit opportunities for environment and self-contamination Outside front of the PPE is the area most likely to be contaminated . Perform hand hygiene after PPE removal THANK YOU Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) issues regulations for workplace health and safety. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) issues recommendations for when and what PPE should be used to prevent exposure to infectious diseases. General rules of PPE use Don before contact with the patient. Use carefully – don’t spread contamination. Remove and discard carefully . Immediately perform hand hygiene. Factors to consider Type and degree of exposure anticipated Splash/spray versus touch Category of isolation precautions Durability and appropriateness for the task Fit or availability of correct size. Selection of PPE TYPES OF PPE Gloves – protect hands. Masks and respirators (N95)– protect mouth/nose. Gowns/aprons – protect skin and/or clothing. Goggles – protect eyes. Face shields – protect face, mouth, nose, and eyes. Head cover – protect head (hair) & forehead. SURGICAL MASK Indications of use Protect HCWs nose and mouth from splashes or sprays of large droplets. SURGICAL MASK How to don a surgical mask? Perform Hand hygiene Find the top side of the mask (nose piece up) Place over nose, mouth and chin to cover the face Fit flexible nose piece over nose bridge Secure on head with ties or elastic Fit the mask to your face and under your chin. Adjust to fit without leaving gaps on the sides SURGICAL MASK How to doff a surgical mask? Perform Hand hygiene Untie the bottom, then top, tie Pull the face mask forward off the face to remove. Discard in medical waste Perform Hand hygiene

name: Infographic: PPE Reference
text: SEQUENCE FOR PUTTING ON PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT (PPE) CS250672-E The type of PPE used will vary based on the level of precautions required, such as standard and contact, droplet or airborne infection isolation precautions. The procedure for putting on and removing PPE should be tailored to the specific type of PPE. 1. GO WN • Fully cover torso from neck to knees, arms to end of wrists, and wrap around the back • Fasten in back of neck and waist 2. MASK OR RESPIRATOR • Secure ties or elastic bands at middle of head and neck • Fit flexible band to nose bridge • Fit snug to face and below chin • Fit-check respirator 3. GOGGLES OR FA CE SHIELD • Place over face and eyes and adjust to fit 4. GL OVES • Extend to cover wrist of isolation gown USE SAFE WORK PRACTICES TO PROTECT YOURSELF AND LIMIT THE SPREAD OF CONTAMINATION • Keep hands away from face • Limit surfaces touched • Change gloves when torn or heavily contaminated • Perform hand hygiene HOW TO SAFEL Y REMOVE PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT (PPE) EXAMPLE 1 There are a variety of ways to safely remove PPE without contaminating your clothing, skin, or mucous membranes with potentially infectious materials. Here is one example. Remove all PPE before exiting the patient room except a respirator, if worn. Remove the respirator after leaving the patient room and closing the door. Remove PPE in the following sequence: 1. GL OVES • Outside of gloves are contaminated! • If your hands get contaminated during glove removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Using a gloved hand, grasp the palm area of the other gloved hand and peel off first glove • Hold removed glove in gloved hand • Slide fingers of ungloved hand under remaining glove at wrist and peel off second glove over first glove • Discard gloves in a waste container 2. GOGGLES OR FA CE SHIELD • Outside of goggles or face shield are contaminated! • If your hands get contaminated during goggle or face shield removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Remove goggles or face shield from the back by lifting head band or ear pieces • If the item is reusable, place in designated receptacle for reprocessing. Otherwise, discard in a waste container 3. GO WN • Gown front and sleeves are contaminated! • If your hands get contaminated during gown removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Unfasten gown ties, taking care that sleeves don’t contact your body when reaching for ties • Pull gown away from neck and shoulders, touching inside of gown only • Turn gown inside out • Fold or roll into a bundle and discard in a waste container 4. MASK OR RESPIRATOR • Front of mask/respirator is contaminated — DO NOT TOUCH! • If your hands get contaminated during mask/respirator removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Grasp bottom ties or elastics of the mask/respirator, then the ones at the top, and remove without touching the front • Discard in a waste container CS250672-E OR 5. WASH HANDS OR USE AN ALCOHOL-BASED HAND SANITIZER IMMEDIATEL Y AFTER REMOVING ALL PPE PERFORM HAND HYGIENE BETWEEN STEPS IF HANDS BECOME CONTAMINATED AND IMMEDIATEL Y AFTER REMOVING ALL PPE HOW TO SAFEL Y REMOVE PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT (PPE) EXAMPLE 2 Here is another way to safely remove PPE without contaminating your clothing, skin, or mucous membranes with potentially infectious materials. Remove all PPE before exiting the patient room except a respirator, if worn. Remove the respirator after leaving the patient room and closing the door. Remove PPE in the following sequence: 1. GOWN AND GLOVES • Gown front and sleeves and the outside of gloves are contaminated! • If your hands get contaminated during gown or glove removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Grasp the gown in the front and pull away from your body so that the ties break, touching outside of gown only with gloved hands • While removing the gown, fold or roll the gown inside-out into a bundle • As you are removing the gown, peel off your gloves at the same time, only touching the inside of the gloves and gown with your bare hands. Place the gown and gloves into a waste container CS250672-E A B D E C 2. GOGGLES OR FA CE SHIELD • Outside of goggles or face shield are contaminated! • If your hands get contaminated during goggle or face shield removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Remove goggles or face shield from the back by lifting head band and without touching the front of the goggles or face shield • If the item is reusable, place in designated receptacle for reprocessing. Otherwise, discard in a waste container 3. MASK OR RESPIRATOR • Front of mask/respirator is contaminated — DO NOT TOUCH! • If your hands get contaminated during mask/respirator removal, immediately wash your hands or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer • Grasp bottom ties or elastics of the mask/respirator, then the ones at the top, and remove without touching the front • Discard in a waste container OR 4. WASH HANDS OR USE AN ALCOHOL-BASED HAND SANITIZER IMMEDIATEL Y AFTER REMOVING ALL PPE PERFORM HAND HYGIENE BETWEEN STEPS IF HANDS BECOME CONTAMINATED AND IMMEDIATEL Y AFTER REMOVING ALL PPE

text: Measuring and Recording Blood Pressure Aneroid Sphygmomanometer Aneroid means “without fluid,” and as the name suggests, this type of BP apparatus doesn’t make use of any mercury and is therefore considered the safest alternative to mercury sphygmomanometers. In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. There is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Why do we use Stethoscope? Stethoscope Try to put your stethoscope on your radial or brachial artery would you hear anything? Korotkoff sounds What we would here Systolic Diastolic = 120 80 Maximum pressure First sound to hear after releasing pressure of cuff Least pressure Last sound to hear while deflating cuff https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTJvWLi2uCM So let us measure the blood pressure https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6HtqolhKqo&t=44s Before the procedure Wash hands Introduce yourself Explain procedure Explain to the patients they might feel discomfort from the cuff but not painful Patient position Setting down on chair if they can after 5 minutes rest Back , leg and arm supported Ask the patients to expose the right arm by rolling up their sleeves What is blood pressure? Attaching cuff Should be right size Deflated 2cm above antecubital fossa Measuring blood pressure First method is: Palpatory method to get estimated (rough value ) systolic blood pressure Palpate the patient’s radial pulse Inflate the blood pressure cuff until you can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. Note the reading on the sphygmomanometer at the point at which the radial pulse becomes impalpable ( this point is estimated systolic blood pressure) Deflate the cuff till zero Close the valve Measuring blood pressure Second method is: Auscultatory method to get actual systolic and diastolic reading Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery pulse, ensuring that it does not touch the cuff. Inflate the cuff to 20-30 mmHg more than the estimated systolic blood pressure (obliteration pressure). Then slowly deflate the cuff at around 2-3 mmHg per second The first consistent Korotkov sounds indicate the systolic blood pressure. text: Vital Signs Radial Pulse Vital signs are indicators of the basic functions of body. A ny physiological or pathological changes in the body functions would be reflected on the vital signs The 4 main vital signs routinely checked by healthcare providers include: Body temperature Pulse rate Breathing rate (respiration) Blood pressure We will start by pulse rate What is pulse rate ? Pulse Rate: is measuring heartbeat by palpating a peripheral artery by the fingertip . The pulse rate is a measurement of the heart rate. This is the number of times the heart beats per minute. As the heart pushes blood through the arteries, the arteries expand and contract with the flow of the blood. Taking a pulse not only measures the heart rate, but also can indicate the following: Heart rhythm Strength of the pulse The normal pulse rate for health adults ranges from 60- 100 beats per minute. Exercises, some illness and emotions could increase the heart rate. On the other hand, runners who do a lot of cardiovascular conditions may have slower heart rate with 40 beats per minute. Pulse could be recorded from accessible arteries such as: C arotid T emporal B rachial R adial How to measure Radial pulse ? STEP CP P A NP Getting ready Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds. Wash hands Greet the patient, Stand on the right side, Introduce yourself to the patient, and Explain the procedure to the patient. Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm on his chest. The procedure Use the right hand to palpate the patient's left radial pulse and vice versa. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, about two centimeters proximal to the thenar eminence . Place the tips of the index, middle and ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel. Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: if regular, count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and if irregular, count for 3 minutes and divide by 3. After the procedure Wash the hands. Discuss the findings with the patient. Record the results as beats / minute and comment on regularity. Thank the patient. CP: Competently performed P A performed with A ssistance NP ( not done) II. Arterial Blood Pressure What is Blood Pressure Blood pressure is defined as the lateral pressure exerted by flowing blood on the walls of the arteries How is blood pressure measured? Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and is given as 2 figures: systolic pressure – the pressure when the heart pushes blood out diastolic pressure – the pressure when the heart rests between beats What are equipment needed for measuring blood pressure Sphygmomanometer There are different types of Sphygmomanometers Mercury Sphygmomanometer Mercury sphygmomanometers are made up of manually inflatable cuffs that are attached to measuring units with mercury-infused tubes. While operating the device, it is important to place the apparatus on a flat surface and in an upright position to get the correct readings. Aneroid Sphygmomanometer Aneroid means “without fluid,” and as the name suggests, this type of BP apparatus doesn’t make use of any mercury and is therefore considered the safest alternative to mercury sphygmomanometers. In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer The automatic digital sphygmomanometer is the most technologically-advanced sphygmomanometer design to date. These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. Similar to mercury and aneroid sphygmomanometers, digital sphygmomanometers also come with inflatable cuffs, but there is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Unlike the other two types, automatic digital sphygmomanometers evaluate and measure the fluctuations of arteries. Stethoscope III. Measuring Blood Pressure STEP/TASK CP AP NP Getting ready: Wash your hand Introduce yourself to the patient. Explain the procedure and obtain his consent. Tell him that he might feel some discomfort as the cuff is inflated, and that the blood pressure measurement may have to be repeated. Position The patient should be in the sitting position after 5 minutes rest. Three parts should be supported: back, feet and the arm. Ask the patient to expose the right arm by rolling up sleeve Attaching Blood Pressure Cuff Check that the blood pressure cuff size is appropriate for the patient's arm and that it is fully deflated Confirm the location of the brachial artery by palpating medial to the biceps brachii tendon and lateral to the medial epicondyle of the humerus Wrap the blood pressure cuff around the patient's upper arm, 2 cm above the antecubital fossa. Measuring blood pressure Position the BP measuring device so that it is roughly at the level of the patient’s heart. Position the measurement column/dial so that it is at eye level. Position the patient's right arm so that it is horizontal at the level of the midsternal and free from obstructive clothing. Measuring Blood Pressure Palpatory method Palpate the patient’s radial pulse, Inflate the blood pressure cuff until you can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. Note the reading on the sphygmomanometer at the point at which the radial pulse becomes impalpable. This reading is an approximate estimate of the patient's systolic blood pressure Open the valve and deflate the blood pressure cuff Close the valve on the blood pressure cuf f Measuring Blood Pressure Auscultatory Method Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery pulse, ensuring that it does not touch the cuff. Inflate the cuff to 20-30 mmHg more than the estimated systolic blood pressure (obliteration pressure). Then slowly deflate the cuff at around 2-3 mmHg per second The first consistent Korotkov sounds indicate the systolic blood pressure. The muffling and disappearance of the Korotkov sounds indicate the diastolic blood pressure. Record the blood pressure as the systolic reading over the diastolic reading. If the blood pressure is higher than 140/90, indicate that you might take a second reading after giving the patient a one minute rest. If the patient has a history of postural hypotension. you must also record the standing blood pressure To complete the procedure Once the blood pressure has been obtained, remove the blood pressure cuf f. Explain to the patient the procedure is complete Discuss the blood pressure results with the patient, including any further steps that may need to occur (e.g., follow-up, further investigations, initiation of treatment) Thank the patient Wash your hands Figure . Positioning of the cuff and head of the stethoscope Figure . Positioning of the cuff and head of the stethoscope

name: Vital Signs: Pulse
text: Review Learning Guides for Measuring Radial Pulse before clinical skills session on Vital Signs Radial Pulse Vital signs are indicators of the basic functions of the body. Any physiological or pathological changes in the body functions would be reflected in the vital signs . The four main vital signs routinely checked by healthcare providers include: Body temperature Pulse rate Breathing rate (respiration) Blood pressure We will start by pulse rate What is the pulse rate? Pulse Rate: is measuring heartbeat by palpating a peripheral artery with the fingertip. The pulse rate is a measurement of the heart rate. This is the number of times the heart beats per minute. As the heart pushes blood through the arteries, the arteries expand and contract with the blood flow . Taking a pulse not only measures the heart rate but also can indicate the following: Heart rhythm Strength of the pulse The normal pulse rate for healthy adults ranges from 60- 100 beats per minute. Exercises, some illnesses and emotions could increase the heart rate. On the other hand, runners who do a lot of cardiovascular conditions may have a slower heart rate of 40 beats per minute. Pulse could be recorded from accessible arteries such as: Carotid Temporal Brachial Radial How to measure Radial pulse ? STEP CP PA NP Getting ready Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds. Wash hands Greet the patient, Stand on the right side, Introduce yourself to the patient, and Explain the procedure to the patient. Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm on his chest. The procedure Use the right hand to palpate the patient's left radial pulse and vice versa. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, about two centimeters proximal to the thenar eminence. Place the tips of the index, middle and ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel. Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: if regular, count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and if irregular, count for 3 minutes and divide by 3. After the procedure Wash the hands. Discuss the findings with the patient. Record the results as beats / minute and comment on regularity. Thank the patient. CP: Competently performed PA performed with Assistance NP ( not done)

name: Read Me first: Course syllabus
text: Course Description Form Course code Course Name Course prerequisites MED11CS1 clinical skills 1 - Course description clinical skills 1 offers an early clinical exposure for year 1 students through introduc ing them to basic clinical and procedural skills needed for year 1. Through this course students will become aware of rules and regulations in clinical skills lab , safety measures and what is expected from them in this course . The course provides opportunities for students to practice basic clinical and procedural skills for year 1 students . Clinical skills 1 course is taught along semester 1 twice weekly . Course aim This course aims to introduce students in year 1 to basic clinical and procedural skills such as hand hygiene, donning and doffing Personal P rotective E quipment, principles of history taking and patient consultation and finally recording vital signs such as pulse and blood pressure. Course objectives By the end of this course, students will: Identify different types of Hazards Relate different types of signs to biohazardous infectious materials Reflect on the importance of hand hygiene Discuss WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene Perform effective hand hygiene in 30 seconds Don and doff personal protective equipment in right order Describe different items for history taking Take a thorough general history from standardized patient Discuss the indication for recording vital signs Mention different vitals signs Measure and record radial pulse of left arm of Simulated Model with precision 4 from actual measuring Measure and record radial pulse of standardized patient with precision 4 from actual measuring Measure and record blood pressure both palpatory and auscultatory on right arm of Standardized patient using mercury sphygmomanometer with precision 10 mmHg from actual measuring. Measure and record blood pressure both palpatory and auscultatory on simulated model using aneroid sphygmomanometer with precision 10 mmHg from actual measuring. Reflect on their performance Develop action plan for future performance taking into consideration instructor feedback and self-reflection Course topics Simulation lab tour, rules and regulations Hospital Safety Measures Hand Hygiene Personal Protective Equipment History Taking Vital signs 1: Measuring and recording radial pulse Vital Signs 2: Measuring and recording Blood pressure References https://www.who.int/campaigns/world-hand-hygiene-day course lecture notes and learning guides
